column3: “solitary as an oyster” (1) → “A solitary child, neglected by his friends” (2) → “the neglected grave” (4).
column4: The schoolboy connects solitary with neglected; the grave repeats neglected.

column3: Scrooge: “Are there no prisons?” / “And the Union workhouses?” (1) → Christmas Present: “Are there no prisons?” / “Are there no workhouses?” (3).
column4: Scrooge’s argument is returned to him.

column3: “they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population” (1) → “he had better do it, and decrease the surplus population”, applied to Tiny Tim (3).
column4: An abstract judgement acquires a particular victim.

column3: Scrooge: “It’s not my business” → Marley: “Mankind was my business.” (1)
Belle: “A golden one” (2) → Bob describing Tim: “As good as gold” → the Cratchits’ cups serving “as well as golden goblets would have done” (3).
column4: Wealth, human goodness and the value of ordinary things.

column3: “no steel had ever struck out generous fire” (1) → the schoolboy’s “feeble fire” (2) → “Make up the fires” (5).
column4: Emotional warmth connects with material comfort.

column3: “I wish to be left alone” (1) → “I have come to dinner. Will you let me in, Fred?” (5).
column4: Rejecting company becomes asking to belong.

column3: The collector: “You wish to be anonymous?” (1) → Scrooge about the turkey: “He sha’n’t know who sends it.” (5)
column4: The collector’s question anticipates Scrooge’s later gift.

column3: “Tiny Tim upon his shoulder” (3) → Mrs Cratchit remembers Bob walking “with Tiny Tim upon his shoulder, very fast indeed.” (4)
column4: An ordinary action becomes a painful memory.

column3: “the child will die” (3) → “Tiny Tim, who did not die” (5).
column4: A warning becomes an averted outcome.

column3: “I was a boy here!” (2) → “I am as merry as a school-boy” → “I’m quite a baby.” (5)
column4: Remembered childhood develops into renewed joy and possibility.
column5: It should also be noted that the book is like a coming of age tale where the character gets younger
